title: Fragmentation Entropy vs Slot Efficiency — Mini benchmark notes
body:
Goal:
Measure how slotization fragmentation (measured via a simple 'fragmentation entropy' metric) maps to effective slot utilization (ESU), latency percentiles, and per-token cost across three candidate allocation strategies. This is exploratory — lightweight synthetic bench to inform an A/B for Q3.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- Fragmentation Entropy (FE) correlates with p99 inflation and dollars/1M tokens (stronger effect on cost than p90).
- Adaptive tiling + compacting pass reduces FE by ~35% vs fixed small slots and recovers ~18% ESU (best cost/p99 tradeoff in our workload mix).
- Multiplex opportunistic mode gives very good p90 at low load but suffers tail jitter under microbursts (p99 blow-up).

Definitions (used in analysis):
- Slot: scheduling unit on GPU (capacity for N tokens per scheduling epoch).
- Effective Slot Utilization (ESU): tokens_processed / slot_capacity over 1m window (0..1).
- Fragmentation Entropy (FE): Shannon entropy over the distribution of slot fill fractions f_i (normalized): FE = -sum(p_j log2 p_j) where p_j = fraction of slots with fill in bucket j. We bucket fill fraction into 8 bins (0-12.5%, 12.5-25%, ...). Intuition: higher FE means more spread/fragmentation in how full slots are — harder to pack.

Experiment setup:
- Synthetic session mix: 60% short (10-50 tokens), 30% medium (80-300 tokens), 10% long (600-1,200 tokens).
- Concurrency pattern: Poisson arrivals with bursts (30s windows) and baseline lambda tuned to generate 75% average GPU occupancy for baseline.
- Models: redwood-small-v1 (3B equiv), redwood-mid-v2 (7B equiv) — quantized paths used for cost measure. Batch size caps and queueing same across strategies.
- Strategies compared:
  1) fixed-small-slots: uniform slot size = 128 tokens, naive assignment.
  2) adaptive-tiling: slot sizes chosen by recent session length histogram (per-minute retiling) + compact pass every 60s to merge underfilled slots when safe.
  3) opportunistic-multiplex: aggressive multiplexing across many small contexts, best-effort packing, preemption allowed for higher-priority sessions.
- Metrics captured: ESU, FE, p50/p90/p99 latency (ms), dollar_cost_per_1M_tokens (simulated cost model: GPU-minutes + amortized infra), slot-preemption count, and tail jitter (p99-p90).

Results (representative numbers — 95% CI over 6 runs):

ASCII table:
| Strategy               | ESU  | FE (bits) | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | p99-p90(ms) | $/1M tok | notes                       |
|------------------------|------|-----------|---------|---------|---------|-------------|----------|-----------------------------|
| fixed-small-slots      | 0.62 | 2.95      | 48      | 122     | 410     | 288         | $122     | simplest, high fragmentation|
| adaptive-tiling        | 0.73 | 1.92      | 52      | 136     | 220     | 84          | $100     | best cost, moderate p90     |
| opportunistic-multiplex| 0.68 | 2.40      | 40      | 98      | 520     | 422         | $140     | best p90, worst tail/cost   |

Interpretation notes:
- FE tracks inversely with ESU: lower entropy => more concentrated slot fills => higher ESU. Adaptive-tiling reduced FE by ~35% vs fixed-small-slots, recovering ~0.11 ESU.
- Despite slightly higher p50/p90 for adaptive-tiling compared to opportunistic, p99 is much better (220ms vs 520ms) — tail behavior dominates $/1M tok because long tail causes more slot time retention and retries.
- Opportunistic multiplexing is attractive when the workload is dominated by very short interactions and microburst amplitude is low; under bursty patterns it accumulates preemptions and fragmentation leading to high p99 and costs.
- Fixed-small-slots are simple but leave tokens unutilized (many slots at low fill) which increases GPU time per useful token processed.

Visual (compact): latency sparklines (p99):
- fixed-small-slots: |||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||| (410 ms)
- adaptive-tiling:   |||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||| (220 ms)
- opportunistic:     |||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||| (520 ms)

Correlation snapshot (Pearson r, across per-minute windows):
- FE vs p99: r = 0.72 (strong positive correlation)
- ESU vs $/1M tok: r = -0.81 (higher ESU -> lower cost)

Edge cases observed:
- Long-session heavy tail (>=1000 tokens) flips advantage: adaptive-tiling sometimes increases p90 because of extra work to rebalance tiles; but p99 still improves because long sessions are packed more predictably.
- Multiplexing preemption count spikes during burst windows leading to transient queue thrash; this shows as jitter in p99-p90.

Recommendations (practical):
1) Instrument FE and ESU in the Console as two cheap signals (per host/pool, 1m aggregation). Add FE to the recommended dashboard for Dedicated pools.
2) For mixed workloads like ours, default scheduler should prefer adaptive-tiling + 60s compact pass. Route opportunistic-multiplex as an opt-in runtime knob for latency-sensitive but predictable short-session customers.
3) Implement a lightweight nightly compaction maintenance for low-risk pools (merge partially used slots during low-traffic hours) — expected to cut FE by additional ~10% in production trace replay (estimate).
4) Add a canary: enable adaptive-tiling on 10% of capacity for 2 weeks and monitor p99, ESU, $/1M tok, and customer-error-rate.

Data caveats and open questions:
- Synthetic session mix may not reflect actual customer sidebands (e.g., many chat apps have higher long-session tail). Need a short trace replayer on real production traces (sampled, anonymized) to validate magnitudes.
- Cost model here is simple; actual $/1M tokens depends on bin-packing of multi-tenant artifacts and infra overheads not modeled.
- FE bucketization (8 bins) chosen for interpretability. Need to test sensitivity to bin count (4/16) and different entropy bases.

Action items (owners):
- Asha: wire FE/ESU metric in observability-telemetry prototype (dashboard + 1m rollups) — due 2026-06-30.
- Diego: implement compact-pass prototype in tile allocator PR (github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1109) — WIP, finish by 2026-07-07.
- Marta: run 2-week replay against 10% canary with real traces and produce postmortem (metrics + cost delta) — start 2026-07-10.

Notes-to-self: prioritize quick telemetry (makes decisions visible), avoid premature optimization of multiplex scheduling until we validate preemption costs on real traffic.

References: lightweight derivation of FE metric (internal note), related linear ticket and runtime PR (linked_artifacts above).

End of mini-report.
